Question: Find the smallest integer \(n\) such that \[ \begin{aligned} (x^2+y^2+z^2)^2 &\le{}\\[-4pt] &n(x^4+y^4+z^4) \end{aligned} \] for all real numbers \(x,\) \(y\) and \(z.\)
Solution:
Equal values provide a useful first test because all three variables enter symmetrically. Setting \(x=y=z=1\) in the required inequality gives
\[
9\le 3n,
\]
so any valid integer must satisfy \(n\ge3\). It remains to prove that \(3\) works for every real triple.

Compare the two sides by subtraction. Expanding and collecting terms gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&3(x^4+y^4+z^4)-(x^2+y^2+z^2)^2\\
&\qquad=(x^2-y^2)^2+(y^2-z^2)^2+(z^2-x^2)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every term on the right is the square of a real number, so the difference is nonnegative. This proves the required inequality with \(n=3\) for all real \(x,y,z\), including the all-zero triple.

Equality holds exactly when all three squared differences vanish, or \(x^2=y^2=z^2\). In particular, the test triple \((1,1,1)\) attains equality and rules out every smaller integer. Hence the smallest integer is \(\boxed{3}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
